values.value: • Use the past engagement as proof, but do not assume this deal will close on relationship alone. • Review what worked, what did not, and what the customer wants improved this time. • Bring adoption data, outcome data, or user feedback from the earlier engagement. • Position the next purchase as a logical expansion, renewal, or upgrade with fresh value. • Ask what would make this round easier and faster for the buyer to approve.
2|Repeat purchase
Buyer may say, 'This time it is different.' Response: 'That is useful to know. Let us keep the trust from the last engagement, but rework the value story for what has changed now.'
Use the earlier win to speed up trust. Bring proof of value, adoption, and what will improve this time.
Low risk. Use past success to expand faster.
Say: 'Last time, these were the outcomes. This round, we can improve speed, scale, or coverage.'
Repeat purchase

• Help the buyer shape the business case instead of only selling product. • Clarify first-phase scope, success metric, target audience, and implementation owner. • Reduce perceived risk with a phased rollout or pilot path. • Tie the initiative to institutional goals, workforce readiness, compliance, productivity, or learner outcomes. • Make it easy for the buyer to explain internally why this should be funded now.
2|New Initiative
Buyer may say, 'We are still exploring.' Response: 'That is fine. Let us define what a successful first phase looks like so the exploration becomes useful and decision-ready.'
Shape the buying vision early. Help them define the business case, rollout logic, and first-win outcome.
Risk: New initiatives stall if the case for change is weak.
Ask: 'What does a successful first phase look like, and who will judge that success?'
New Initiative

• Diagnose what is not working in the current setup before positioning your alternative. • Understand pain points in adoption, quality, platform experience, support, analytics, or commercial value. • Show a low-friction transition path with minimal disruption. • Build a switching story around better outcomes, not only price. • Prepare a side-by-side comparison that makes change feel safe and practical.
2|Total / Partial replacement of current solution
Buyer may say, 'Changing vendors is painful.' Response: 'Agreed. That is exactly why I would like to show a low-risk transition path rather than just a better-looking proposal.'
Win by exposing gaps in the current setup, then show a safer switch path. Focus on pain, transition, and business impact.
Risk: Replacement deals become price fights without a switch story.
Ask: 'What is not working today, and what would make a change worth the effort?'
Total / Partial replacement of current solution

• First find out if this is repeat spend, new budget, or a switch from an existing provider. • Ask what triggered the conversation and whether there is an incumbent or current internal workaround. • Understand if the buyer is expanding, replacing, or exploring. • Adjust your sales motion only after the opportunity type is clear. • Without this clarity, avoid pitching a generic solution.
2|Don't know
Buyer may say, 'We are figuring that out ourselves.' Response: 'Understood. If I know whether this is expansion, fresh spend, or replacement, I can guide you much more accurately.'
First understand whether this is expansion, new spend, or replacement. The sales motion changes based on that answer.
Risk: Wrong positioning because the deal type is unclear.
Ask: 'Is this a fresh budget, an expansion, or a move away from an existing vendor?'
Don't know
What is the opportunity type?
